question: When Church, kings and merchants start to write fats down, what do their rules and ledgers show about oil, butter and the whale?
summary: The Middle Ages divide Europe by fat. For roughly half the year Christians fast, and in the north, where butter and lard are the cooking fats, a Lent without butter is a hardship; in the south oil carries on ([[b1]]). Councils forbid butter in Lent, a duchess lobbies Rome for the right to use it in 1491, and a cathedral tower is said to have been paid for out of butter dispensations ([[o1]], [[o2]], [[b2]]). Butter itself shifts from a sheep's luxury to an everyday cattle fat ([[ec5]]), and oil serves as money in the south ([[ec6]]).

Documents also make other fat economies countable. The Cairo Geniza shows Tunisian oil shipped to Egypt by the skin, Egypt's flax, linseed and sesame oils, and a trade in linseed oil east to Aden ([[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[x2]]); the Song capital counts oil among the seven necessities, with a dozen oils listed, tallow-tree candles, and the first Chinese description of an oil press ([[ec4]], [[th1]], [[te2]], [[te1]]); and the Basques hunt right whales from about AD 1000, selling the blubber as ‘Lenten fat’ until kings begin to tax the whale ([[ec1]], [[o3]]).
Two quieter shifts close the folio: palm oil is on sale on the West African coast by the 1480s ([[ec7]]), and, in China, su drifts from butter toward animal-fat shortening ([[ec8]]).

themes.title: Lent, butter and the oil line
text: The Church's fasting rules, their enforcement and their sale: a geography of fats written into law, built tower by tower.

themes.title: The Mediterranean oil ledgers
text: Geniza documents show the real flows: Tunisian oil to Alexandria, Egyptian linseed to Syria and Aden, sesame in the Delta.

themes.title: Song China's oil economy
text: A dozen oils, the first described press, candles from the tallow tree and a changing meaning for su.

themes.title: The Basque whale and the beginning of whale-oil
text: The first organised whaling, sold for fast-day fat and light and soap, quickly taxed by kings.

turning_points.text: The Basques hunt the right whale and sell its fat on fast days.
Five thousand skins of Tunisian oil reach Alexandria in one season.
Wang Zhen describes the Chinese oil press.
The Council of Angers restricts butter in Lent.
The Butter Tower of Rouen is built.
Brittany, then much of northern Europe, wins butter dispensations.

how_to_read: *Order* and *Belief* carry the Lent story; *Economy* and *Exchange* carry the Geniza and the Song. The Nexus ties the fasting rules to the butter dispensations and the whale taxes.
The two halves of the folio (Latin Europe and the Islamic and Chinese worlds) barely touch, and the Overview reads them side by side.

sources.intro: Documents rule this period. The Geniza, the Song miscellany and the Lenten canons are all read through intermediaries — Goitein, Needham and Khosrova — and so inherit their selection.
main: Khosrova, with Flandrin, for Lent and butter ([[b1]], [[o1]], [[o2]], [[b2]]); Mueller for oil as money ([[ec6]]).
Goitein, *A Mediterranean Society* vol. 1, read by OCR, for the Geniza ([[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[x2]], [[l1]]).
Needham, SCC 6.5, for Song and Yuan China ([[ec4]], [[th1]], [[te1]], [[te2]], [[ec8]]).
Ellis for whaling ([[ec1]], [[o3]]); Lynn for palm oil ([[ec7]]).
contested: The Rouen tower's financing is tradition without accounts ([[b2]]); the date of the Angers canon is not given ([[o1]]).
Mueller's oil-as-money contracts are unnamed ([[ec6]]); the Butter-to-cattle shift is unsourced ([[ec5]]).
The Muslim scholar's remark on Jewish cake makers is hostile testimony ([[l1]]).
gaps: Medieval Italian, Spanish and Provençal oil trade, and soap guilds, have no primary source here.
Vol. 3 of Goitein and Ibn Butlan, Seth and Ibn al-Baytar on fats were not read for this folio.
